title: King Evander and the Shield of Aeneas

blocks.text: All of Italy was getting ready for war against the Trojans. Aeneas did not know where to find help. He lay down by the river Tiber, worrying, and at last he fell asleep.
In his dream, an old man rose up out of the river, wearing a blue robe and a crown of reeds. It was Father Tiber, the god of the river.

"Welcome to my land, Aeneas," he said. "Don't be afraid of this war. Here is a sign for you. When you wake, you will find a huge white pig lying on the riverbank, with thirty white piglets. And here is where to find help. Upriver lives a king named Evander, who came here long ago from Greece. He is always at war with the Latins. Go to him, and make him your friend."

When Aeneas woke up, there on the riverbank lay a great white pig with thirty white piglets, just as Helenus had promised long ago. So Aeneas took two ships and rowed up the river. Father Tiber held back his current, so that the river was as smooth as a pond and the rowing was easy. They glided along under the shady trees, and at noon they saw a little town on a hill.

That day King Evander and his people were holding a feast for Hercules outside the town. When they saw strange ships coming through the trees, they were frightened and jumped up. But Evander's son, young Pallas, grabbed a spear and called out bravely, "Strangers, who are you? Do you come in peace or in war?"
Aeneas held up an olive branch. "We are Trojans," he called. "We have come to ask King Evander to be our friend."

Pallas took his hand and led him to his father. And when the old king looked at Aeneas, he smiled. "I know your face," he said. "You look just like your father, Anchises. I met him long ago, when I was a young man, and he gave me a beautiful quiver of arrows and a cloak woven with gold. Of course I will help you. Tomorrow I will send you off with all the help I can. But today, join our feast."
So they feasted together. And when they had eaten, King Evander told them why they were holding a feast for Hercules.

"Do you see that great heap of broken rocks on the hill?" he said. "There used to be a cave there, deep in the cliff, and in it lived a monster called Cacus. He was half a man, and he breathed fire and smoke, and he was the terror of this land.

"One day the hero Hercules came this way, driving a herd of magnificent cattle, and he let them graze in the valley by the river. That night Cacus crept out and stole eight of the finest cows. He was clever. He dragged them backward by their tails into his cave, so that their hoof prints pointed the wrong way. Then he rolled a huge stone across the door.
"In the morning, Hercules was getting ready to leave. As his herd moved off, the cows mooed. And from deep inside the cave, one of the stolen cows mooed back!

"Hercules grabbed his great club and ran up the hill. Cacus was terrified. He ran into his cave and dropped the huge stone in front of the doorway. Hercules pushed and pulled, but he could not get in. So he went around to the top of the hill, where a great rock leaned out over the river, and he pushed it with all his strength until it crashed down into the water. Now the whole cave was open to the sky!

"Cacus breathed out clouds of fire and smoke to hide himself. But Hercules jumped right down into the cave, into the thickest of the smoke, grabbed the monster and held him tight until Cacus was beaten for good. Then he dragged the stolen cows out into the daylight. And that is why we hold a feast for Hercules every year, to thank him for saving us."

Then the priests sang songs about the great deeds of Hercules: how he strangled two snakes when he was only a baby, how he killed the lion of Nemea, and how he went down to the underworld and dragged out the three-headed dog Cerberus.

In the evening, they walked back to the little town, and Evander told Aeneas about the land. "Long ago," he said, "wild people lived here in the forests, with no laws and no farms. Then the god Saturn came here, when his son Jupiter took his throne in the sky. Saturn taught the people to live together, and gave them laws. His time was called the Golden Age, because everyone lived in peace."

As they walked, Evander showed Aeneas the hills and the woods and the places where his cattle grazed. Aeneas did not know it, but they were walking on the very ground where one day the great city of Rome would stand. Where cows mooed in the grass, there would one day be palaces and temples of gold.

Evander's palace was small and plain. "Hercules himself stayed in this little house," he said. "So don't be too proud to stay here. Try to be like him, and care more about being good than being rich." And he gave Aeneas a bear skin to sleep on.
Early the next morning, Evander came to see Aeneas, with two dogs trotting at his heels.

"My kingdom is small," he said. "I cannot give you much help. But not far from here there is a great people, the Etruscans, who have just thrown out their cruel king, Mezentius. Mezentius has run away to join Turnus, and the Etruscans want to fight him. But a prophet told them, 'No man of Italy can lead you. You must wait for a leader from across the sea.' You are that leader! Go to them. And I will send my son Pallas with you, with my best horsemen, so that he can learn how to be a soldier from you."

At that moment, thunder rumbled in the clear blue sky, and they heard a trumpet sound high above. They looked up and saw shining armor flashing among the clouds. It was a sign from Aeneas's mother, Venus.

When Pallas rode away beside Aeneas, old Evander held his son tight. "If the gods bring you back safe to me, my son," he said, "I will be glad to live on. But if not, I would rather die now, while I still have you in my arms." And he was so sad that he fainted, and his servants carried him inside.
Meanwhile, Venus had gone to her husband Vulcan, the god of fire and the blacksmith of the gods. "Please," she said, "make armor for my son Aeneas."

So Vulcan went to his workshop on a smoking island near Sicily, where the Cyclopes were busy hammering thunderbolts for Jupiter. "Stop that work," he told them. "We must make armor for a hero." And they made Aeneas a helmet with a crest that blazed like fire, and a sword, and a breastplate of bronze, and a spear, and a shield.

The shield was the most wonderful thing of all, because on it Vulcan made pictures of the future, the whole story of Rome. There was the she-wolf lying in a cave, gently licking the twin babies Romulus and Remus, who were not afraid of her at all. There was brave Horatius holding the bridge against an army, and Cloelia swimming across the river. There were the geese of the Capitol, flapping their silver wings to warn that the enemy was coming. And there were many more battles, and heroes, and great ships fighting on a sea of gold with silver dolphins playing in the waves.

Venus brought the armor to Aeneas, where he was resting alone in a valley, and laid it at his feet. "Here are the gifts I promised you," she said. "With these, you need not fear anyone, not even Turnus."
Aeneas was delighted. He put on the armor and lifted the great shield onto his shoulder. He did not understand the pictures on it. But he was carrying the whole future of Rome.

A simplified retelling of Alfred J. Church's “King Evander and the Arms of Aeneas” in Stories from Virgil (1879). The original is listed under Other versions. Church spells the hero's name “Æneas” and uses Hercules, the Roman name for Heracles.
